newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Britain's schools become pre-election battleground.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Britain's schools become pre-election battleground.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major left state school at 16 and worked his way up to lead a Conservative party run by an elite educated in exclusive private academies.

Opposition Labour leader Tony Blair went to Fettes College, the select Edinburgh school known as Scotland's Eton, and then to Oxford University -- the classic route to establishment power -- before taking control of a party committed to equality in education.
Given this, it is hardly surprising that differences between Labour and the Conservatives on education have shrunk, but the issue will still be a hot one in this year's general election.

"Increasingly Labour is trying to be as much like the Conservatives as it can," said Stephen Pollard, a former head of research at the Labour-affiliated Fabian Society think tank who quit after a row over school policy.
Labour, attacking Conservative policy as socially divisive, disputes this bitterly.
In a country whose middle class grew wealthier in the 1980s, only to be gripped by insecurity about the future in the 1990s, education has become a key political battleground.
LABOUR MAKES EDUCATION TOP PRIORITY
Labour leader Tony Blair has vowed to make education his priority if, as polls suggest, he wins Britain's forthcoming election, which is now at most four months away.
Blair told BBC television he wanted to pursue education reform with the same vigour as former Conservative prime minister Margaret Thatcher overhauled Britain's union laws.

"In the late 1990s, and early part of the next millenium, I want the next Labour government to be every bit as committed and determined and passionate about driving through education reform in this country," Blair said.
After 18 years in the political wilderness, Labour needs the middle class votes that have given the Conservatives four consecutive terms in office.

To win them over Blair has shredded old dogmas in an unprecedented drive to modernise Labour and dismayed traditional supporters by vowing not to kill off schools that select their pupils via competition for places.
In another U-turn, Blair agreed schools should have more control over their own affairs, an idea championed by Major.

Even Blair's education spokesman David Blunkett -- a left-winger dedicated to equal opportunity who was written off as a pupil at a school for the blind and whose own children go to an inner-city comprehensive -- fell into line.

Blunkett unveiled plans for public/private partnerships to repair schools and effectively endorsed -- although with fine-tuning -- Major's introduction of league tables to monitor and grade school performance.

To wrest control of traditional Conservative rhetoric, Blair has pledged to sack substandard teachers, close poor schools, set minimum homework requirements and punish parents who fail to control their children.
LABOUR TRADITIONALISTS OUTRAGED

Blair's campaign on education has won him possibly more enemies than in any other policy area. They have homed in on his decision to send his son to a school which has opted out of local authority control, rather than a local school.
But Blair, who has said his children's future will not be sacrificed to political correctness, has faced them all down.

His political control did not waver when his social security spokeswoman, Harriet Harman, went even further and sent her son to a school with a competitive entrance policy -- a system deemed elitist by traditional Labour supporters.
Her open defiance of party policy against pupil selection led to hundreds of Labour faithful sending back their membership cards. But Blair backed her and Harman stayed.
The casualty in all this has been Labour's traditional, cosy relationship with the teaching unions.
This has served to reinforce Blair's aim -- to put Labour on the side of parents at the school gates worried by what they see as low standards and poor teaching.
Labour's shift has left Major with a dilemma.
TORIES LACK WEAPONS TO FIGHT BACK

After almost a decade in which the government has introduced a national curriculum, begun national tests for children and encouraged schools to opt out of local authority control, the Conservatives are short of new ideas to fight back.
One of the government's new schemes -- nursery vouchers designed to counter Labour's plans for free nursery places for three and four year olds -- is having a shaky start.

The government watchdog, the Audit Commission, has warned the scheme will need careful monitoring to prevent fraud and has questioned whether it will in fact expand nursery provision in areas where it is lacking -- echoing Labour criticism.
Fighting back, Major has pinpointed selection and parent choice as the defining issues between himself and Blair.

Overruling his Education Secretary Gillian Shephard, who argued for consolidation after years of dramatic change, Major called for a "grammar (high quality) school in every town" and for more schools to be able to select their pupils.
But he immediately ran into fire from one of Britain's leading commentators on education, Sir Claus Moser, who said he was dismayed by Major's approach.
"It is all about politics, not about children. Labour policy statements are freer of political dogma," Moser, a former head of the government's statistical service, said last year.
COST CONCERNS RISE
But there was a sting in the tail. Moser said Labour would have to boost education spending by at least 3 billion pounds ($5.02 billion) a year to raise levels of literacy and numeracy.

Labour has been coy about the cost of its plans, except to say that it would fund a reduction in primary school class sizes by scrapping the assisted places scheme, which subsidises children from poorer families who attend private schools.
Stripping aside the rhetoric, educationalists say money is the key question for both parties.

"The great weakness with the policies of the Labour party and the Conservative government is they are very unwilling to tell us how they're going to pay for it all," said Alan Smithers, professor of policy research at Brunel University.
"You can see the reluctance... Some of the plans look OK on paper. But quite where the engine -- the money -- is going to come from, I don't know," Smithers said.
